The traditional model is usually a single string, with the pitch changed by pushing or pulling the pole to alter the string's tension. To begin, steady the plucking first, then practise pushing and pulling the pole hard and soft to control the pitch; the tea-chest bass is also mainly plucked, and the number of strings can be increased as needed.

Its range sits in the bass, it can produce a rumbling, muffled sound, and the span of pitch is comparatively limited. The resonance of the metal tub gives it a particular response, so the timbre carries a metallic ringing tail. Against the traditional double bass the washtub bass is rougher and more homely, lacking refined musicality but full of the plain character of a folk instrument. Its sound is like a mixture of percussion and strings — the continuous pitch of a string with the overtones of percussion — and it is an indispensable rhythmic and bass foundation in American folk music.

The washtub bass is a chordophone used in American folk music, with a metal washtub as its resonator. The traditional form is usually a single string: the player pushes or pulls a wooden pole or stick to change the string's tension and so tune it, and plucks to sound it. It is common in the jug bands of early African American communities and was also used in the old-time folk music of Appalachians of European descent; in the 1950s British skiffle bands used the tea-chest bass variant, and in the 1960s American folk musicians used it in music influenced by the jug bands.
這件樂器用於美國民謠與水罐樂團，二十世紀初在紐奧良非裔美國人社區流行，後於曼菲斯: This instrument is used in American folk music and jug bands. It was popular in African American communities in New Orleans in the early twentieth century and later flourished in Memphis and Louisville; Appalachians of European descent also used it in old-time folk music. British skiffle bands use the tea-chest resonator variant, and similar bass instruments appear in Australian and New Zealand bush bands and in South African kwela bands. Jug bands of the 1960s American folk revival took it up again, and it can be heard on recordings such as "Poorboy Shuffle".
